entry.summary: FrameRate Showcases now offer six layouts, a visual editor and personal invites with analytics, so you can pitch clients and see exactly what they watched.
entry.content:

You send a list of links to your videos. The producer writes back, “Thanks, I’ll take a look.”

Then nothing. Did they open it? Which pieces did they watch? Did they come back for a second look?

Showcases on FrameRate now tell you, down to the play count. (They also make your work look far better than a list of links ever could.)

We've just shipped a major update to Showcases. Tyler walks through everything in the video above. Here's the rundown.

Six layouts to choose from

The biggest change is choice. Every Showcase can now use one of six layouts, each with its own look and feel. That way the presentation fits the project, not the other way around.

Grid. A clean grid of your work with room for a logo, a title, and (new) a description. Click a video to watch it. If you've allowed downloads, viewers can grab files directly from the Showcase.

Grid with hero. Same grid, plus a large image or video across the top. Ideal when one piece should lead.

Horizontal scroll. Your title and description stay fixed on the left while viewers scroll through the work sideways.

Horizontal split. Title up top, description at the bottom, and the work scrolling through the middle.

Vertical carousel. Your title and description hold their place on the left while the work moves top to bottom, one piece after another. It's one of Tyler's favorites.

Gallery. The original layout is still here. The selected video takes center stage, with thumbnails underneath so viewers can jump between pieces.

A visual editor

We also rebuilt how you make a Showcase. The editor is now much more visual. You can edit the title and description right on the page and add videos.

Switching layouts takes one click from the menu at the top, and you see the result immediately.

To reorder your work, open the Videos tab and drag everything into place.

More control in Settings

Under Settings you'll find a full set of controls:

  • Upload your own logo and adjust its size (it carries across all your Showcases)

  • Password protect a Showcase

  • Autoplay videos one after another

  • Turn on looping

  • Turn downloads on or off

  • Enable theater mode

Invites and analytics

You can now send a Showcase directly to a specific person.

Enter their name and email, and FrameRate creates a unique invitation just for them. You can also see at a glance whether they've viewed it.

The payoff is what happens next. With analytics, you can see when someone opens your Showcase, which videos they watch, how many times they play them, and whether they download anything.

No more wondering if the producer ever clicked your link.

Built to help you win the work

Our goal with Showcases is simple: give you a better way to present your work. Something that looks professional, feels like you, and helps you land your next client.

If you've been presenting work through Wiredrive, Simian, Shots, or Vimeo Showcase, this is a good moment to take another look. Showcases live right alongside your FrameRate hosting and client review tools, so everything stays in one place.

Head to Showcases in your account, click Create, and try the layouts for yourself.

entry.content:

We spend our lives chasing the creative spark.

Sometimes the chase is a joyous adventure of discovery, illuminating what we’re capable of.

Sometimes it leads us into shadows of doubt, with no guarantee of a payoff.

But we don’t really have a choice. We chase it wherever it goes. It’s the curse and the destiny of the creative spirit.

At least, that’s my interpretation of this festival opener from The Heist for this year’s Half Rez in Chicago. Like any good work of art, it leaves enough room for each viewer to find their own meaning.

The process

Just as important as the film itself is the process behind it. The Heist used the project as an opportunity to bring together the studio’s wide range of talents through equal parts storytelling and experimentation.

From their Study on FrameRate:

…the work moved through Cinema 4D, Houdini, Procreate, After Effects, Blender, and Rive, with each tool helping solve a different part of the story.

The real fun was in figuring out how those worlds could connect, and how we could connect more easily while making them.

Music plays a huge role, too. Sanctus Audio’s playful, curious score becomes a through-line for the hero spark, adding depth and texture without overwhelming the film. The sound design is tastefully understated, yielding to the acoustic instrumentation and the music’s evolving sense of wonder.

Like the festival it opened, the film captures much of what makes motion design special: the intersection of creativity and technology, curiosity and discovery, deep collaboration and deeply personal desires and dreams.

entry.title: Sculpting Time: The Art of Editing
entry.summary: Editor Dave Conte on the craft of cutting animation, surviving client notes, and his award-winning work on Love, Death + Robots.
entry.content:
Dave Conte is an editor whose work spans commercials and animation, including award-winning episodes of Love, Death + Robots.

We asked him what editing really is, how animation rewires the job, and how to survive your worst client notes.

What is the role of an editor?

At its core, we are storytelling problem solvers.

The problem: How do we turn all of these assets we’re given into a story that holds viewers’ attention?

My favorite comparison I like to make is that our work is analogous to that of a sculptor. Editing follows a similar subtractive principle, our giant block of marble is the hours of footage that we chisel down into a functional edit.

We’re basically time sculptors.

What I love about editing, and what can be daunting about it, is that the possibilities are virtually endless. Especially with animation, where you aren’t bound to the stuff you shot.

The only limit (besides time and money) is the imagination of the creatives. Every frame you choose to cut or keep will yield a new edit.

How does editing animation differ from editing live action?

With live action, you are often given all of the footage you’re ever going to get up front. You have the entire giant block of marble right from the beginning, and the edit is pretty malleable until the very end of the process. Lots of “what if we tried this take” instead.

Animation is both more freeing and more restricting, with a heavier creative lift up front for the editor.

You’ll often start with nothing but storyboards that you need to cut into a boardomatic, with the hope being that you end up with a solid timing ref before things go to animation.

This can (and should!) involve finding temp music, sound effects, and recording scratch VO to make the boardo feel more like a complete piece. Those endless possibilities I mentioned earlier feel particularly endless here.

The animatic phase is similar, except now we’re more zoomed in, working with each shot as a series of frames instead of a single storyboard. Here is where the most small-scale timing adjustments will take place.

Usually I’ll receive a PNG sequence of a shot, and I’ll lay out each individual frame to time out the motion for the animators to then refine on their end.

This is ideally when any final dialogue/VO is recorded, since it’s easier to build the pacing around the dialogue, rather than try to shoehorn it in later. No VO artist wants to be told “match the scratch.”

With live action, refinements and re-edits are pretty much always on the table until finishing, and even then, nothing is truly ever “locked” in this world.

With animation, the story and the timing needs to be hammered out much earlier in the process, with not a lot of wiggle room for adding new shots, or drastically changing existing ones later on.

Once the animation timings are locked, the editorial lift becomes much lighter, with most time spent updating shots with new versions as they come in, refining sound design before going to mix, and prepping for eventual finishing and delivery.

You won awards for your work on Love, Death + Robots. What made those projects unique or challenging?

Those were two of the coolest projects I’ve ever worked on, and they were unique for a whole host of reasons.

The directors gave me a lot of creative freedom to explore, and I spent a lot more time than usual on sound designing the boardomatic, including doing a ton of voice acting to help nail the humor.

Since everything was sped up to sell the mini-ness of it all, I had to account for how that would affect comedic timing across the various scenes.

The biggest challenge was the creative burnout that tends to crop up on projects with long timelines.

Both of those episodes took about a year and a half to edit from start to finish, at varying intensities, with other team members working on it even longer than that.

With commercials, I’m often bouncing from one project to the next every few weeks, so it was interesting to see how burnout can hit even for a project I love and am extremely proud of.

What advice would you give to folks just getting started in their editing careers?

Don’t take notes personally, and don’t get too attached to anything that isn’t yours.

Client work is for the client, and they wouldn’t have hired you if they could do it themselves.

You WILL get awful, stupid, downright nonsensical notes from your clients all the time. Notes that go against the fundamentals of editing (I’ve lost count of how many J-cuts I’ve had shot down because “the sound comes in too early”). It’s how you deal with those notes that keeps them from coming back.

The golden rule in film is “show, don’t tell,” and in that spirit, I’m a fan of the A/B edit, where you present one edit pretty much exactly as requested by the client, and another that you add more of your editorial sensibilities to.

It doesn’t always go the way you want, but it shows initiative and creativity, and is a good exercise in how to find the middleground.

And when they DO go with your version, it often comes with more trust in your creative process, as well as a much-needed ego boost.

Learning when and how to push back is a skill that takes time to develop. Push back and/or complain too much, and you’ll be labeled as tough to work with. Push back too little, and you’ll set a bad precedent that can sap the confidence of your creative team.

Ultimately, you’re in charge of how you react to “make it go faster.”

Do you have a favorite editor?

It goes without saying that Thelma Schoonmaker is the best to ever do it, and her work has inspired me for decades.

But one of my personal favorites is Skip MacDonald.

His work on Breaking Bad, Better Call Saul, and Fargo should be studied for how effectively he builds tension without being showy.

He mostly guides the narrative with a deft, invisible hand, but he’s also maybe the best montage editor alive. And when Skip gets an opportunity to peacock, everybody wins.

Also a huge fan of fellow LDR editor Kirk Baxter. I feel like he is an extension of David Fincher’s voice the way Thelma is with Marty.

His work on The Social Network alone is worth a spot on the all-time great list, but everything he’s done with Fincher, and how his editing has elevated his work, is inspiring stuff.

entry.title: Introducing Studies: The stories behind the work
entry.summary: Share the thinking and process behind your work with FrameRate Studies
entry.content:
What are Studies?

No job is a straight line from start to finish.

Behind every tidy 15-second video is a pile of false starts, rejected ideas, discarded shots and late-night conversations that never see the light of day.

Some of that work was rooted in rigorous strategy. Some of it was an artistic impulse that took you somewhere you didn’t expect.

Both are worth showing.

A finished piece shows people what you made.
The process shows them how you think.

That’s what a Study is for.

And on FrameRate, you can share that thinking with a community of people who care deeply about the craft.

The anatomy of a Study

A Study is a custom page about a single project, and you build it out of blocks.

Start with a hero for the project title and cover. Add individual media, media grids, body copy, pull quotes, stats, section headings, dividers and credits.

Media grids come in several layouts, including masonry for when your frames refuse to be the same shape.

Link a credit to someone with a FrameRate account and they’ll be notified, just like they are with video credits.

Native Rive support

If you’ve ever had to show interactive Rive work as a screen recording, Studies give you a better option.

Drop a .riv file into a Study and it runs live in the page, the way you built it.

See it in action

You decide who sees it

Every Study is Public, Unlisted, or Private.

Public Studies can appear on the Explore page, on the FrameRate homepage and on your profile, and anyone can read them without an account.

Unlisted Studies work for anyone with the link but stay out of discovery, which makes them useful for things like pitches and presentations. On Plus plans and above, you can also password-protect them.

Private Studies are visible only to you.

Flexible by design

Studies are meant to be flexible containers for your creativity.

The building blocks give you room to mix writing, images, video and native Rive animations, while the layouts keep the page looking clean and considered.

Beyond that, what you make with them is up to you.

  • Oddfellows “This is Figma”

  • James Ramirez “Into the Spider-Verse”

  • Abraham E. “Noodlz”

Studies are available on every plan, including Free. The only limit is your storage, the same pool your uploads already use.

entry.summary: The best Vimeo alternatives for filmmakers, motion designers, editors, VFX artists, and animators in 2026.
entry.content:
If you're a filmmaker, motion designer, animator, VFX artist, or editor and you've decided it's time to leave Vimeo, here's where to go.

Six platforms, ranked, with the reasons and the trade-offs.

What happened to Vimeo

For about 15 years, if you made moving images for a living, your work lived on Vimeo. Not because it was the cheapest host or had the best features, but because that's where everyone else's work lived too.

You'd post a piece. A few people whose work you admired would leave a comment. Every so often the Staff Picks team would put a little laurel next to your name, and your inbox would fill up.

Vimeo was our campfire. We gathered around a shared light to see and celebrate what everyone else had made.

That fire has been dwindling for a decade. Vimeo pivoted toward enterprise video around 2016 and never really looked back.

Then, in September 2025, the company agreed to sell itself to Bending Spoons for $1.38 billion. The deal closed in November.

In January, the new owners laid off most of the company, including nearly the entire video engineering team.

Who is Bending Spoons?

If you don't know them, here's the short version: they buy well-known software (Evernote, WeTransfer, Meetup, StreamYard, Brightcove, and most recently AOL), cut staff aggressively, and raise prices.

It's not a secret. It's their business model, and they're proud of it.

I'm not going to speculate about what that means for Vimeo specifically.

I'll just point out that the pattern has been consistent, and that the features you probably care about most (removing Vimeo branding from your player, customizing how your embeds look) already sit behind the $25-a-month Standard plan, which is $41 if you pay monthly.

So yeah. It's tough out there.

About that number one spot

You're reading this on FrameRate's blog, and FrameRate is the first entry on the list. I'm not going to pretend that's a coincidence.

What I will say is that I've tried to be fair to everyone else here. If one of them is the better fit for you, I'd rather you know that than sign up for the wrong thing and leave in a month.

The short version

If you don't want to read 2,500 words, here's the list:

1. FrameRate for creatives who want their work seen and taken seriously by other creatives, with client Reviews, Case Studies, and Showcases built in. Ad-free, full player control, real community. Free plan with 500 MB; paid plans starting at $10 a month.

2. YouTube for maximum reach, if you can live with ads on your embeds and an algorithm that isn't on your side. Free.

3. Frame.io for review and approval during production, not for showing finished work. Free tier is a trial; paid plans starting at $15 per seat per month.

4. Wistia for marketing teams who need analytics and lead capture. Clean ad-free player, no community. Free tier with 25 GB; paid plans starting at $79 a month.

5. Bunny Stream for self-hosting video on your own portfolio site. Pay per gigabyte, no platform, no audience.

6. Behance for a static portfolio where video is one element among many. Free.

Prices are as published in August 2026 and will drift. Check before you commit.

Most working creatives will end up using two of these: one for the production pipeline and one for the finished work. The rest of this post is about figuring out which two.

1. FrameRate

Best for: Filmmakers, motion designers, animators, VFX artists, and editors who want a home for finished work, and studios who need to share, review, and present that work to clients.

Why it exists

FrameRate launched in 2026, and it exists for one reason: the people who make the most carefully crafted video in the world didn't have a place to put it anymore. Not a place that was about that work, anyway.

YouTube is about attention. Vimeo is about enterprise. Frame.io is about the pipeline.

Nobody was building for the person who spends three weeks on a twelve-second shot and wants it seen by someone who understands what that took.

So we built it.

(FrameRate founder Tyler Williams previously built and sold Motion Array. I spent years running Motionographer and working at BUCK and Psyop. Between us, we've been on every side of this problem.)

What you get

You upload your work and it looks the way you intended it to look, on FrameRate and in every embed, because you control the player.

There are no pre-roll or post-roll ads, ever. Your uploads are never used to train AI models, which is written into the policy rather than implied by the vibe.

And there's a community on the other side of the upload button: other people who make things, who leave comments that are worth reading, and who can message you directly.

The tools beyond hosting

Showcases let you assemble work into collections, which is the difference between a pile of videos and a portfolio.

Reviews give you a private space to share cuts with clients and collect frame-accurate feedback without emailing links around.

Case Studies, the newest addition, let you put the finished piece next to the process behind it: the sketches, the styleframes, the tests, the dead ends. That's the thing a reel can't do.

A reel shows you what someone made. A Case Study shows you how they think.

All of that, including Reviews, Case Studies, and Showcases, is available on the free plan.

Watch out for

If you need live streaming or an enterprise sales team, we're not your platform.

If you're a working creative who wants your work to live somewhere that respects it, come say hi.

Price

Free plan with 500 MB of storage; paid plans start at $10 a month on annual billing.

Head over to the pricing page for the full breakdown.

2. YouTube

Best for: Reach. If the goal is the largest possible audience, nothing else on this list is close.

Why it's here

Let's get the obvious one out of the way. YouTube is free, it's everywhere, and it's where people go to look for things.

If you're building a following, teaching, or trying to get a personal project in front of people who don't already know your name, you should probably be on YouTube whether or not you use anything else.

Why you're reading this post instead

Embedded YouTube videos carry YouTube's branding, YouTube's recommendations, and YouTube's ads. Your carefully graded brand film ends with a grid of thumbnails for videos you'd never want next to your work.

The platform's entire design is built to move the viewer to the next thing, not to let them sit with yours.

The community is real, but it's not your community.

If you've spent more than five minutes on YouTube, you know that the comment section there is a very different place than the comment section on a platform where every viewer is also a maker.

Watch out for

Ads on embeds, recommendation overlays, limited player control, and an algorithm that rewards volume and watch time over craft.

Also, YouTube's terms allow the platform to use uploaded content to train its AI models, which you may or may not be okay with.

Price

Free.

3. Frame.io

Best for: Review and approval during production. Frame-accurate comments, version stacking, camera-to-cloud, and deep integration with Premiere Pro and After Effects.

Why it's here

A lot of people leaving Vimeo were using Vimeo's review features. If that's you, Frame.io is the obvious upgrade for the production side of things.

Adobe bought it in 2021 and has kept investing. The current version handles camera-to-cloud workflows, frame-accurate annotation, and the kind of version management that makes a 14-round client review survivable.

What it isn't

A place to show finished work. There's no public profile, no discovery, no community. Frame.io is where the work happens, not where it lives afterward.

Think of it as the edit bay, not the gallery.

Watch out for

Per-seat pricing adds up fast for studios, and the free tier (2 GB, 2 users, 2 projects) is really a trial.

If you're a freelancer who mostly needs to send a cut to one client and collect notes, it may be more muscle than you need.

Price

Free plan; Pro starting at $15 per seat per month; Team starting at $25 per seat per month.

4. Wistia

Best for: Marketing teams who need to know exactly who watched what, for how long, and what they clicked afterward.

Why it's here

Wistia is a fine product aimed squarely at a different person than you. It's built for the marketing department: heatmaps, lead-capture forms inside the player, CRM integrations, A/B testing on thumbnails.

If your job is generating pipeline for a SaaS company, Wistia is excellent at that.

Why it's probably not for you

If your job is making the video, most of that is dead weight. You'd be paying for analytics infrastructure to host a showreel.

The player is clean and customizable and there are no ads, which is why it shows up on every Vimeo-alternatives list. But the free tier is small and the first paid tier is a real jump.

Watch out for

The pricing model. Business is $79 a month on annual billing ($99 monthly) and includes three users; extra users are $25 each.

There's no community and no discovery of any kind, because that's not what it's for.

Price

Free plan (25 GB storage, 200 GB bandwidth); Business starting at $79 a month on annual billing.

5. Bunny Stream

Best for: Creatives who already have their own portfolio site and just want to host the video files somewhere fast and cheap.

Why it's here

This is the do-it-yourself option.

Bunny isn't a platform in the sense that the others are; it's video infrastructure. You upload files, it encodes and delivers them over a global CDN, and you embed the player on your own site.

Storage is about a penny per gigabyte per month, delivery is a fraction of a cent per gigabyte, and encoding is free. For a portfolio site with a few dozen videos and modest traffic, you could easily spend less than a coffee a month.

The price of that price

You're on your own. You're building the portfolio page, handling the design, maintaining the site, and there's no one on the other end.

No comments, no profile, no chance that someone whose work you admire stumbles onto yours.

Bunny is a very good answer to "where do I put the file." It is not an answer to "where do I put the work."

Watch out for

It assumes you're comfortable with a developer-flavored dashboard and a bit of embed code.

Bandwidth pricing varies by region. And if your site goes down, so does your reel.

Price

Pay-as-you-go, roughly $0.01/GB storage and $0.005/GB delivery, with a $1 monthly minimum.

6. Behance

Best for: A static portfolio where video sits alongside stills, boards, and process images.

Why it's here

Behance is Adobe's portfolio network, and for a lot of designers it's already the default. It has a real community with real discovery, and for a project that's mostly styleframes and illustration with a bit of motion, it works.

You can present the whole thing as a project page with process images, which is the right instinct.

The catch

Behance is an image-first house and video is a guest in it. There's no real video player to speak of, no embed control, and no sense of a piece of film as the primary artifact.

Motion designers tend to use Behance for the boards and link out to somewhere else for the animation. That "somewhere else" is the whole reason this post exists.

Watch out for

Direct video uploads are capped at 1 GB and a maximum width of 1280 pixels, which in 2026 is a limitation somewhere between quaint and disqualifying.

Behance's own help center suggests hosting the video on YouTube or Vimeo and embedding it instead. So you'll still need one of the platforms above.

Price

Free, technically. The homepage only offers a Pro trial ($9.99 a month), and the way to get a free account is to click "Sign In" as if you already had one.

Once you're in, the "Share Work" button is where new projects live.

None of this is hidden exactly, but it's not obvious, either.

How to choose

Ask yourself one question: who is the video for once it's finished?

If it's for clients during production, you need a review tool. That's Frame.io, or FrameRate's Reviews if you'd rather keep review and presentation in one place.

If it's for the general public, you need reach. That's YouTube, and it's fine to hold your nose about the ads.

If it's for a marketing funnel, that's Wistia, and you probably weren't reading this post anyway.

If it's for your own site and nothing else, that's Bunny, plus a weekend of building.

If it's for the people who will actually understand what you made, the people you'd want to hire, be hired by, or just be seen by, that's what FrameRate is for.

That was the gap. Vimeo used to keep that fire going, then walked away from it. We'd like to tend it for a long time.

Moving your work

A few practical notes for the migration, regardless of where you land.

Download your originals first

Vimeo lets you download the source files you uploaded, and you should do that before anything else, because you don't know what next year's Vimeo looks like. Store them somewhere that isn't Vimeo.

The FrameRate Migrator tool will let you download your Vimeo library with no strings attached. You can optionally upload to FrameRate with all your folders, tags, and privacy settings in tact. But no pressure.

Find every embed

Make a list of every place your videos are embedded: your portfolio site, your studio's site, client sites, old blog posts.

Those embeds will break when you close your Vimeo account.

Don't close Vimeo yet

Let it lapse to the free tier if you like, but leave it up until you've swapped every embed.

Rebuild deliberately

A migration is a chance to cull. The work from 2014 that you're keeping for sentimental reasons can live on a hard drive.

But if you're a pack rat by nature, no judgment here. We have plenty of folks with a couple thousand videos sitting in their FrameRate libraries, just waiting for their moment in the sun.

Frequently asked questions

Is Vimeo shutting down?

No. Vimeo is still operating and Staff Picks still updates daily.

What's changed is who owns it, how many people work there, and what the owners have historically done with the companies they buy.

Whether that's a reason to leave is a judgment call.

What's the best free Vimeo alternative for filmmakers?

For pure reach, YouTube. For a home for finished work without ads, FrameRate's free plan gives you 500 MB of storage with no expiration and access to Reviews, Case Studies, and Showcases.

Wistia and Frame.io both have free plans, but they're closer to trials than tiers.

Which alternative has a community like Vimeo used to?

FrameRate is built specifically around that: a place where the audience is made of other people who make things, with comments, direct messages, and curation that celebrates craft rather than engagement.

YouTube has a community, but it's a general one (and infamously nasty at times).

Behance has one, but it skews toward still image-making. It also requires an Adobe ID to sign up, which is either a non-issue or a dealbreaker depending on how you feel about Adobe.

Can I use an alternative for client review?

Yes. Frame.io is the industry standard for review during production.

FrameRate's Reviews cover the same ground for finished cuts: private, shareable links with frame-accurate comments.

Which platforms don't train AI on my videos?

FrameRate has an explicit no-AI-training policy for uploaded work.

YouTube's terms allow Google to use uploaded content for machine learning. For the others, read the current terms carefully; these policies change and are often buried.

Do I need to pick just one?

Almost certainly not. The most common setup for a working creative is a review tool for the production pipeline plus a home for finished work, and maybe YouTube for personal projects that want an audience.

FrameRate is a video platform built for filmmakers, animators, editors, VFX artists, and motion designers.

entry.title: How do you make seven films at once without losing your mind?
entry.summary: Making one animated film is hard. Brut Works made seven at once. Here's how the studio pulled it off.
entry.content:
Making one animated film is hard. Making seven at once, each inspired by a different artist's work and rooted in Canary Islands lore, is the kind of job most studios would politely decline.

Brut Works said yes.

In the words of Executive Creative Director & Founder, Martin Allais, here's how they pulled it off.

Seven artists, seven stories, and seven different animation approaches. This sounds like a dream project and a massive undertaking at once. 

Did you have doubts about whether you could pull it off?

In a lot of ways it was a dream project. In many others, a nightmarish black hole. But we saw the potential. 

It also wasn't very clear how much creative freedom there would be or what stories were going to be portrayed. We pitched this in Q4 2024 and we started producing in spring 2025, so it was a big question mark. 

It was very risky to jump in so blind, but we felt something was different, and that alongside the fact that it's rare for us to work for Spain made it the right fit. 

We never had doubts about whether we could pull it off. It was more like, could we pull it off and stay alive!

Collaborations require deep trust with your creative partners. How did you build trust with your collaborators?

At Brut Works, we work as a creative studio but also as a collective. The majority of the artists are people we've known for years and we're used to collaborating with. 

The partnership with the agency was a first, and the key for that was openness and respect. We were upfront about the challenges and explicit about our process. 

That bonded the relationship and we were able to overcome all the challenges and get a good experience out of the project.

The agency brought in an outside expert to fact-check the storytelling, since these films draw on the real mythology and cultural heritage of the Canary Islands. What was that process like, and what did you learn from it?

The agency brought in the expert because of the institutional character of the campaign. We couldn't invent anything that wasn't grounded in the history and geography of the islands because it would have meant losing credibility. 

We bought books and got deep into the identity of the islands. It's always refreshing when a project forces you to research beyond the technical and leaves you with more substance in your soul than when you started it.

You helped select the seven artists. How did you choose them?

We proposed a lineup of artists to the agency early on in the process. For us it was about different styles harmonizing together in one campaign. 

The client was committed to representing diverse voices and connecting with Canarian artists, so we puzzled that together with them. 

Gender equality and a balance between local and international artists was the axis of it. So laying this criteria on top of our stylistic curation took a long time, around 8 weeks to really nail it down to a point where everybody on the agency and client side felt good about it. (Us, too.)

The final lineup:

  • "El Demonio de Echeyde:" Nicolás Marsá

  • "La Pared de Roberto:" Ciara Quilty-Harper

  • "El Gigante de Mahán:" Sara Herranz

  • "La Princesa Ico:" Carla Garrido

  • "El Árbol Garoé:" Dedo Ciego

  • "La Cuesta de Silva:" Ann Bahrs

  • "Gara y Jonay:" Paulina Mocna

Technically speaking, which of the seven films was the hardest to pull off?

The most difficult and challenging thing for us wasn't any of the films in particular, but the fact that we needed to do all of them at the same time. 

Laying the 7 production pipelines on top of each other was really difficult and not necessarily cost efficient, but way better than doing them one by one. It was very challenging for a studio of our size to take this on, we barely could take other jobs.

Also, when we laid out the production, we decided that in order to make the films cohesive (and possible), we would create storyboards with the main team.

We agreed on rhythm and storytelling before giving it to the artists, so we could make sure we finished successfully and coherently as a whole campaign. Some of the artists didn't have animation experience, so that added complexity to it.

What started as a big challenge became a beautiful bootcamp for creating 7 films that intertwined with different styles and different parts of the story of the islands. Definitely one of a kind.

On the bright side, we grew along the way and we feel stronger and more resilient with big productions now.

Do you have a favorite moment or scene across the series?

At the beginning of the process, our roles were clearly defined. I was directing the studio side and one of our directors, Tomás Peña, was leading the creative. 

Once the job finished preproduction and we started hands on, the work multiplied and we started moving roles. Other directors like Alba Prado and Maliboo started taking over on different films and very organically the collective started to make sense. 

A bunch of heads that can work as a team but also have visions of their own. I got fully immersed in the music, for example, and everybody started jumping into different films organically. It was beautiful.

That can only happen when there is trust and respect. It creates a sense of freedom that is very pleasant to feel, especially under tight deadlines and limited resources where people usually get more stressed. 

Jobs like this remind me why we started this and how we are as a creative force.

I want to thank Tomás Peña, Maliboo, Alba Prado, Nico Marsá, Dedo Ciego and the rest of the collective in the production and studio side for always being hands on and believing in doing things in a different way. Love them for exploring not only ideas, but structures. 

That matters to us because we believe different ways of doing shape different experiences, and those are the ones that imprint your career and resignify what it is to be a creator in this day and age.

Was AI used in creating this project?

This was a project 100% human, with its quirkiness and the imperfection of going into a production with excitement and even a certain naivety. 

We believe human creativity goes first and then tools follow. It's always been that way. 

This is a non-AI project because we could afford it, and we're proud of it, but we understand that this kind of production will be rare in the future, like analog photography or oil painting.

We're glad to have had the opportunity to pull off something like this, and every time we can do it, we will. But we're not against new tools and we will try them and come up with our own versions of it. 

The duty of the artist is to pioneer and build the languages upon which these new tools gain meaning to human creation. Let's not let the wrong people own these spaces and fill them with crap. 

We need to integrate and not divide. Whatever version of the future happens depends on us.

entry.title: FrameRate embeds work everywhere
entry.summary: How to embed FrameRate videos on any website: what the platform dropdown actually does, how to customize the player, and where the code lives.
entry.content:
Here's something a surprising number of FrameRate members don't know: your videos can be embedded anywhere.

Not "anywhere with an asterisk." Anywhere. If a website lets you paste HTML, your FrameRate video will play there.

(Admittedly, we could have been louder about this. Consider this us being louder.) 

So here's how FrameRate embeds actually work, where they work, and how to get the most out of them.

What a FrameRate embed actually is

When you grab the embed code for one of your videos, you're getting a standard iframe that loads our player:

<iframe src="https://framerate.tv/embed/your-video-id" ...></iframe>

That's it. No proprietary script, no SDK, no plugin to install.

The iframe has been a core part of HTML since the first Harry Potter book, and every browser, CMS, and site builder on Earth knows what to do with it.

This means your portfolio site doesn't need to "support FrameRate." It just needs to accept HTML.

The player itself is fully responsive, works in every modern browser (mobile included), and streams at up to 4K.

And it's not a stripped-down version of the FrameRate experience. It's the same player, wearing whatever outfit you choose.

About that platform dropdown

When you open Embed Settings on a video, you'll see a Platform dropdown with options for Webflow, Framer, Squarespace, Cargo, Adobe Portfolio, and WordPress.

Here's what that dropdown actually does: every platform handles pasted HTML a little differently. Some want a responsive wrapper around the iframe. Some have their own container and get confused if you bring your own. 

The dropdown just adjusts the markup so the player sizes correctly on that specific platform. The video and the player are identical no matter what you pick.

So the dropdown isn't a list of the only places FrameRate works. It's a list of places we've pre-solved the quirks for you:

  • Webflow: drop in an Embed element, paste, publish

  • Framer: insert an Embed component, paste into the HTML field

  • Squarespace: add a Code Block, paste

  • Cargo: use a Page Embed module or Custom HTML block (Cargo strips iframes from rich text, so don't paste into a text field)

  • Adobe Portfolio: add an Embed widget, paste

  • Wix: add an Embed HTML element, paste (use the Default option here)

  • WordPress: add a Custom HTML block, paste (Default option here too)

Everywhere else

If your platform isn't on that list, use Default. That's it.

Shopify. Ghost. Readymag. Format. Semplice. A hand-coded site you built in 2011 and are afraid to touch. A React app. A client's CMS you've never heard of.

If it accepts HTML, the embed should work. 

Make it yours

The embedded player is super customizable, giving you control over:

  • Accent, primary, and track colors (solid or gradient)

  • Control bar opacity, padding, and corner radius

  • Which controls appear, from the play button down to picture-in-picture

  • Autoplay, mute, and loop behavior

  • Your own logo on the player

  • Background video mode, which turns off controls and sets autoplay, mute, and loop in one click (perfect for hero sections)

Pro tip: Use presets

If you embed often, save your settings as a preset and every future embed starts from your look instead of ours.

You can also control where your embeds are allowed to live.

Add allowed domains to a video and the embed will refuse to load anywhere else, which is handy when client work needs to stay on the client's site.

One more thing worth knowing: public videos, private videos, password-protected videos, even videos you've hidden from FrameRate entirely all play fine in embeds.

How to get the embed code

  1. Open your Library and click the menu on the video you want to embed

  2. Choose Embed Settings

  3. Pick your platform from the dropdown (or Default)

  4. Customize the player if you like; the preview updates live

  5. Copy the code and paste it into your site

Embeds are included on every FrameRate plan, including Free.

So: your portfolio, your client's site, your studio's homepage, that side project you swore you'd finish this year. Wherever your work needs to show up, it can show up in a player that looks like it belongs there.

If you hit a snag, tell us and we'll help you out. ✌️

entry.title: Do portfolio websites still matter?
entry.summary: Do you still need a portfolio website in the age of Instagram? Yes. Here's how to curate, structure, and design one that shows employers your best work.
entry.content:
A portfolio is a curated collection of your strongest work that showcases the range of your talents, abilities, and interests.

But do portfolio websites still matter?

Short answer: yes.

To get hired, people need to see your work. A portfolio website remains the most effective place where you can present a curated selection of your creative projects.

Even the most successful designers who have massive followings on platforms like Instagram still tend to use portfolio websites. 

What makes a good portfolio website?

Rule Number One: There are no rules. It just needs to work for you.

Step one: Curate ruthlessly

Having a portfolio site is essential, but what makes a site effective comes down to what you include, and just as important, what you leave out.

I was taught an old-school approach of "less is more" when building a portfolio. In other words, your portfolio is only as good as the worst piece in it. You are better off showing 5 awesome projects than 5 awesome and 3 average projects.

First, curate the very best of your work.

I often see students use splash pages that require clicking to reach the work. As an educator, I constantly hear from employers: "just show the work." Don't make it hard for them.

You have seconds to capture someone's attention before they move on, so make sure the first thing they see when landing on your site is compelling. 

Step two: Pick a hero project

The next step is to decide what project you want people visiting your site to see first.

If your site has a homepage with a grid of thumbnails, the top left thumbnail is the project they will most likely click first, at least in Western countries, where we read from left-to-right and top-to-bottom. 

If your site design is stacked with a long scroll of projects from top-to-bottom, clearly the topmost project will be seen first. My suggestion is to show the project that you are most proud of and that best showcases your abilities and interests. 

When deciding the order of the remaining projects, aim for a flow that showcases your aesthetic and technical abilities.

Variety in the sequence of projects introduces contrast and can quickly demonstrate your stylistic range and project types such as illustration, typography, 3D, compositing, cinematography, tactile design, etc.

General tips for website design

Don’t let the design of the website compete with the work you are showcasing. My suggestion is to keep the design of the site clean, simple, and professional. A white, black, or gray background will not interfere with the colors in your projects. 

Typography should be legible and consistent. Consider using a utilitarian typeface with variable weights for your navigation menu, project names, and descriptions. You might also use a display typeface for moments you want to communicate personality.

Make your navigation as simple as possible. No one wants to figure out how to find your work on your website. Make it easy for the viewer.

Students often ask if they should have all their work on a single landing page or create separate menu pages for each type of creative work such as motion, illustration, photography, etc. That is a personal decision.

Broadly speaking, the more items in the menu, the more complex the navigation. I am a proud generalist, so I like to keep all the various types of work I do on a single landing page.

The branding of your portfolio site should reflect your aesthetic/voice, but not overpower the work within.

If you are a student, don’t sweat your personal branding too much. Your name in an elegant typeface can work just fine as a logo. Just keep the design system for your site clean and consistent.

Thumbnails

Thumbnails are the preview images for projects on your portfolio website.

Think of your thumbnails as gift wrapping around a present. Wrapping paper gets you excited to tear it open and examine what is inside. That means you should curate thumbnails to be visually dynamic and compelling.

Look at your project and find a composition that works as a still, GIF, or looping MP4. GIFs and MP4s can work really well as project thumbnails because short looping animations attract the eye.

But an entire grid of thumbnails composed of GIFs might be overwhelming. Another option is to have an animated preview of your project play when rolling over a thumbnail.

Something else to consider with your thumbnails is how they feel next to each other. You want to build a layout that is visually satisfying. Contrast between thumbnails that are side-by-side will help to distinguish projects.

You probably don’t want two thumbnails next to each other that are too similar in color, value, or content. The layout of your thumbnails will influence the flow and order of how projects are viewed, so take your time in designing the most interesting thumbnails for your projects.

Process and case studies

In addition to presenting completed projects on your portfolio website, you also have the opportunity to showcase your process and present case studies.

Another trend I've seen over many years of teaching is that employers enjoy seeing evidence of the creative process. For starters, seeing curated sketches and ideas alongside finished work is fun and interesting.

Showing your concept and design development serves as proof of ability, meaning you arrived at your solution with purpose and intention. It was not just a lucky one-off design that looks great. Including process with your finished work demonstrates your ability to research, ideate, iterate, and refine.

A question I regularly get from students is: “Should I show the finished project or the process first?”

My suggestion is to show the finished work first. Again, you want to attract and hold the viewer’s attention.

Let the finished work impress the viewer and draw them to dig deeper into the project page and process contained within.

The process you choose to showcase should also be curated and tell an interesting story about the project itself. You do not need to show everything.

Also, make sure that you are capturing high quality examples of your process. Nothing is more disappointing than beautiful sketches, ideation, or analog processes that are photographed poorly with a phone.

If your phone images do not look professional, use a scanner. Do some color correction in Photoshop or another app. Treat every aspect of your work professionally from process through completed outcomes.

How we do anything is how we do everything. 

About page

An About page is an opportunity to introduce yourself. There is no single right way to organize this page.

Let your authenticity direct the tone of your About page. Some people include a headshot or a candid photo, while others may present an illustrative or character-driven portrait of themselves. Some choose not to include a portrait at all. 

Value proposition

A brief biography in this section of the portfolio site offers an opportunity to pitch your value proposition to potential employers as well as give a glimpse into your personality.

A value proposition is what you bring to the table in terms of both hard and soft skills.

You can talk about what areas of design you are most interested in and the types of projects you like to create. 

It’s not a bad idea to mention your technical abilities as well. Some people include where they're from, their interests and hobbies, or a bit of humor.

This information gives a potential employer a brief look into who you are and insight into whether you are a good fit for their team.

Contact info

Although it may seem self-evident, make sure to include a way for people to contact you on your website. At a minimum, include a link to your email. 

Students often ask if they should include their phone numbers on their websites. I think that is a personal decision, but you should ask yourself if you are comfortable letting anyone contact you via phone or text.

You can also consider getting a Google Voice number or other separate number for work purposes. 

What about having a social media presence?

For my students, I recommend using social media as a professional tool to share short form projects such as interesting design and/or illustration, refined motion tests, experimental work, and process.

Small works are well-suited for social media because these platforms support a culture of glance media, work absorbed in a second or two as people scroll.

From a portfolio standpoint, a potential employer who likes what they see on your portfolio website will most likely head over to your social channels to see what type of work you post and to get further insight into your personality.

Conversely, a potential employer who likes something you posted on Instagram will find your website link in your bio, and do a deeper dive into your portfolio.

Your portfolio is a living document

Treat your portfolio professionally and strive to design something you are proud of. However, too much perfectionism can paralyze a creative person from getting started.

I like to think of my portfolio as a living document, meaning it changes. The actual form of my portfolio has radically changed over the course of my career and the work within continues to be updated.

Let your first portfolio website be just that: the first iteration.

I often tell my students that I fully expect their portfolio sites to look different in 3 months, 6 months, or a year.

When to update your portfolio site

It really depends on where you are in your career. 

In the beginning, I updated my site whenever I created something new that I was proud of. The updates were pretty frequent until I was regularly booked as a freelancer and turning down work I didn't have time for.

In my experience, a designer stops updating their portfolio once they reach a senior level in their career where they are literally too busy. At that point, the updates come when they want to change roles, get bored, or have a slow period and realize it’s been 5 years since the last update.

To summarize, a portfolio website is your digital presence containing:

  • Completed Projects

  • Process/Case-Studies

  • About/Background Info

  • Contact Info

  • Social Media Presence

As you are building your portfolio website, don’t forget to have fun. Chances are, if you enjoy the process of making your site, the viewer will enjoy looking at it.

About the author

Austin Shaw is a motion designer, educator, and author. He is an Associate Professor of Motion Design at the Rochester Institute of Technology.

entry.title: A person, not a symbol: Nono Ayuso on "The Mexican Dream"

media:content.media:title: A person, not a symbol: Nono Ayuso on "The Mexican Dream"

entry.summary: It looks like a film about immigration. It isn't. Director Nono Ayuso on "The Mexican Dream" for Cerveza Indio, and the human story beyond the politics.
entry.content:
▶ Ver y reproducir video en FrameRate (5:16)

A Mexican worker. The border. A title that plays on the American Dream. 

Before a single frame rolls, you already think you know what this film is going to argue. And you’re probably wrong.

We talked with director Nono Ayuso about telling a specifically Mexican story from an outsider's perspective, and how "The Mexican Dream" sidesteps the obvious narrative of borders and politics.

How did this project come about? Did you have to compete for it, and if so, why do you think it was awarded to you?

The project came through Landia Mexico, the production company that represents me there, and I was fortunate enough to be invited to pitch for it alongside the wonderful team at Ogilvy Mexico.

I pitched for the project in March, but I've never been particularly good at guessing why a job ends up being awarded to me. There are always so many factors involved. 

What I do think resonated was the desire to approach the story from a deeply human and realistic perspective.

The brief could easily have become a film purely about immigration, borders, or politics. What interested me was something more universal and human: sacrifice, dignity, and love.

I wanted to tell the story of a worker not as a symbol, but as a person. Someone with dreams, fears, routines, and a family waiting for him at home. I think that emotional approach connected with both the agency and the client.

You’re based in Madrid, directing a film about a specifically Mexican experience. What did you do to make sure the film felt lived-in rather than observed from the outside?

I think the first step is accepting that you're an outsider. I spent a lot of time listening. The agency shared testimonies, stories, and research, and we spoke with people who live this experience every day.

In a previous life, I worked as an investigative journalist, often reporting from conflict zones, and I think that experience helped me approach the story with curiosity and humility. It taught me to look beyond the headlines and search for the human story underneath.

What struck me was that, despite the political complexity surrounding the border, the people we met rarely defined themselves through that lens. 

They spoke about providing for their families, getting home safely, watching their children grow up, and building a better future. Those were the things that mattered most to them.

At the end of the day, my goal wasn't to explain their experience. It was to honor their stories with honesty, dignity, and respect.

How fully formed was the script when you started working on this? Was it locked, or did it evolve as you started to collaborate with the rest of the team?

The core idea was already there, but the film evolved significantly throughout the process.

For me, scripts are living things, especially when you're working with real environments and authentic human experiences. 

Once we began location scouting, casting, and meeting the people who inspired the story, certain moments felt more truthful and powerful than what was originally on the page.

The overall structure remained largely intact, but many of the details, gestures, and observations emerged through collaboration and discovery. 

Some of my favorite moments in the final film weren't invented in a room; they were found in the real world, simply by staying open and paying attention. That's one of the things I love most about filmmaking, allowing reality to surprise you and ultimately make the story richer.

In a film built on quiet, intimate moments, the sound design carries a lot of weight. What were you after sonically, and how early did sound enter your thinking?

For me, sound is never something that arrives at the end of the process. It's part of how I imagine a film from the very beginning, and especially the music.

The score was crucial. It was composed by the incredibly talented Juan Luqui , co-composer of The Last of Us . From the earliest stages, creating a soundtrack that felt both emotional and atmospheric helped shape the tone and identity of the film.

The challenge was finding the right balance between realism and emotion. Both the sound design and the music needed to remain grounded in the reality of Leo's experience, while also carrying a certain sense of poetry. 

We wanted the audience to feel the weight of his routine and sacrifice, but without ever pushing the emotion too hard. The goal was to create a sonic world that felt honest, intimate, and deeply human.

What was the most challenging aspect of this project for you personally?

I think the biggest challenge was the schedule. We only had about two and a half weeks of prep and production, but this was the first of three films, so the workload was incredibly intense and demanding.

That said, what I remember most is how invested everyone was in the process. From the agency to the production team, there was a genuine passion for telling this story in the best possible way.

When you have that level of commitment from everyone involved, even the most challenging projects become a pleasure to make.

Is there a specific aspect of this project that you are especially proud of? If so, why?

Advertising often rewards bigger gestures, bigger emotions, bigger statements. What I love about this film is that it trusts small moments.

A man waking up before dawn. A look. A routine repeated thousands of times. The note from a loved one waiting in his pocket.

Those details carry the emotional weight of the story. I'm proud that the film allows them to speak for themselves.

You’ve been a journalist, professor, musician, and now a filmmaker. How has your journey influenced your craft today?

More than anything, it taught me to observe. Journalism taught me curiosity. It taught me to listen before speaking and to understand that every person carries a story. Teaching taught me empathy and communication. Music taught me rhythm, emotion and the importance of what happens between the notes.

Filmmaking became the place where all those disciplines met. Today, I still approach every project with the mindset of a journalist. I start by asking questions.

What would be a dream project for you?

Whether it’s a feature film, a television series or a commercial doesn't really matter. What matters is finding stories that feel deeply personal but resonate universally.

The films I love most are the ones that remind us that, despite our differences, we're all searching for the same things: connection, purpose, love and belonging.

entry.title: Making the FrameRate brand manifesto
entry.summary: How The Furrow built a brand film about craft, community, and the creators who make the work worth watching.
entry.content:
Most clients think they know what they want. And they're usually wrong. We were no different. 

Our original goal was to create a simple brand film. You've seen the recipe before:

  • Start with vaguely optimistic electronic music.

  • Introduce the logo as a platonically ideal construction of shapes. 

  • Sprinkle in some slick animations showing off the palette and type system.

  • End with another logo reveal as the music comes to a crisp, satisfying finish. 

Simple. And that's what we wanted. We thought.

But then, during our first meeting with The Furrow, they started doing something really interesting: they asked questions. Things like…

  • Who specifically are you trying to reach with this film? 

  • How are you hoping to change their behavior? 

  • How will this film be used, and where will it live? 

  • What exactly are you trying to say? 

And that reframed everything. Collaborating with The Furrow both broadened our thinking and sharpened it. They brought intentionality to the entire project.

Over the last seven weeks, we went on a deeply satisfying journey together. Here are some of the highlights from that odyssey. 

It's not me, it's you

The first script that I wrote was, in a word, boring. 

It was a traditional approach to a brand rollout, stepping you through the design system created by Studio K via some mildly poetic voiceover. Not bad, but also not great. 

To bust out of the mental bubble we found ourselves in, we invited The Furrow to a Google Doc and penned literally dozens of revisions with them. 

We let ourselves go wild. At one point, I even proposed a script that involved robots sacrificing a marionette at an altar. (No, seriously.)

As we worked through ideas, we realized that anything tied to the current state of the industry was going to read as a time capsule in two years. We wanted something more evergreen than that.

The breakthrough was to address the viewer directly, in second person, about their own work. As the script says:

You've spent hours honing your work.
Perfecting every cut.
Every frame.
Every detail.
That work deserves a new place to call home.
Where craft is the focus.
Where you have full control.
Where community means opportunity.
A place where you belong.

The platform itself never appears. The whole piece is told through visual metaphors, and the closest it gets to a pitch is the idea that FrameRate is a place to belong, not a set of features wrapped in a UI.

Just specific enough

The central tension of the entire film is a balancing act between abstraction and specificity, between metaphor and literalism.

That tension fueled the evolution of the brand's motion direction, letting frame rate, composition, and transition do as much story work as type and color.

The development of the “every frame, every detail” sequence illustrates the point well. 

The Furrow's first pass was a zoetrope-style transition that pays homage to the early days of animation. 

But something about the zoetrope idea wasn't translating. We needed something simpler, something more universally relatable. We asked, “What's the one thing every person in our audience touches every day?” 

The answer was simple: The timeline. Like first loves, everyone remembers their first timeline. (Incidentally, mine was Macromedia Flash 3, circa 1999. 💖) 

The sequence evolved into a playhead crossing the frame as the camera pulls out to reveal the rest of the edit. Abstract enough not to feel like a screenshot. Familiar enough that anyone watching can see their favorite tool reflected back to them.

Frame rate as a storytelling device

If you're an animator, here's a detail you might catch.

The final render is 24 fps, but inside the piece, frame rates are constantly being dialed up and down. Lower frame rates punch up the craft aspect, the intervention of a human hand. Higher frame rates are more about precision and perceived performance.

"Craft" takes on more meaning when you can show it, so The Furrow did.

They photographed crumpled paper for some of the layers and matched the animation to its natural imperfection. The frame rate drops and the artist's hand becomes visible right at the moment the script lands on “craft.”

Immediately following is the 3D sequence, which runs at the full 24 fps and is all about pixel-perfect control and cutting-edge tech. 

Most viewers won't consciously register any of this. That's fine. Those that see it will appreciate it, and for everyone else, it's working at a subconscious level. 

Building a bridge

Speaking of that 3D sequence, it contained its own unique challenge. 

The sequence is about "full control," demonstrated through layered perspective. We needed dimensional space without being too busy, so it wouldn't compete with the adjacent scenes highlighting craft (texture-heavy) and community (color-heavy). 

The real puzzle was animating the camera to keep content locked while transitioning in a way that felt dynamic but expected. This behind-the-scenes clip shows how tricky it got.

A little splash of acid (green)

This film is the first time the FrameRate identity system is being extended into motion. We had essentially three working colors: black, a stack of grays, and a single acid green (#E4F43C). 

The guidelines are explicit that this restrained base exists so user-created work can take center stage. So we tried to apply the same logic to the film.

The Furrow made the acid green do specific work, pointing at what is telling the story in that frame or pulling the viewer's eye to a specific zone of attention.

The community sequence is the one place we let color blow open, which makes conceptual sense. We wanted to reflect the diverse tapestry of talents that you’ll find on FrameRate. 

Curation as creation

It wouldn’t have made sense to make a brand film for a platform that explicitly refuses AI training on uploaded work and then put AI-generated visuals in the film. So we didn't.

All of the footage you see was sourced from stock asset sites. The curation that went into that was a mini-project unto itself. 

First, The Furrow audited the work that's already on FrameRate to get a sense of what our community is actually making. Then, they trawled through thousands of stock clips, looking for footage that stylistically resonated with the findings from their research. 

The final cut features 113 layers from over 500 selects, all intentionally chosen to foster a sense of belonging and familiarity without being predictable or boring. 

(Side note: If we'd had all the time in the world, we would have licensed work from the FrameRate community directly, but logistically that just wasn't realistic. That approach would have created a massive bottleneck and derailed the entire timeline.)

Sound as structure

Wesley Slover at Sanctus Audio scored the film and produced the full mix. The audio direction has its own internal logic that runs parallel to the visual side. 

To find the sound we were looking for, we essentially had a musical conversation, sending references back and forth and discussing what was working and what wasn't over Slack and during live reviews.

I threw Wesley more than one curve ball, often referencing tracks that were only tangentially related to things we’d discussed. Here's a representative excerpt of a Slack conversation:

May 24, 2026
Justin: I was thinking of something a little bit more rhythmic and playful, something that creates opportunity for animation and fun edits while keeping the energy high. 

(I recognize that's different than everything we've discussed up to this point. I'm just wondering what happens if we push the envelope a little?)

Some examples:

  • An extreme example would be something from Antonio Sanchez, like "That's Your Offer?" or  even "Follow Me/America's Population"

  • The sparse instrumentation and playfulness of "Sonata for Cello and Piano in F Minor" (Royal Tenenbaums) is interesting

  • It's too menacing, but the instrumentation and slightly chaotic, percussive quality of "Proven Lands" is... something 😅

Wesley: Yeah I love these references!

I’m interpreting this as aiming to communicate playfulness in creativity and the fun of community. Where I was [previously] thinking warm-fuzzy feelings. Does that seem correct?

As Wesley continued to explore, the cello emerged as a through-line, our platform voice (performed by session musician Jordan Hamilton). Underneath it, a wide range of percussion samples and textures represent the diversity of creators the platform houses.

One consistent voice, many textures.

The sound design pulls heavily from film projector sounds: mechanical, kinetic, historically loaded. (Wesley worked as a film projectionist as a teenager, so there’s a personal connection to all of this.)

Perhaps most importantly, the audio blurs the lines between music and sound design. It’s a distinctively motion design-friendly approach to scoring that established a sculptural process in which the visuals and the audio influenced each other throughout production. 

Chasing recognition, not persuasion

The sentence we kept coming back to in the brief was:

If I care about craft and community, I should be on FrameRate.

We aren’t trying to “sell” to anyone in the traditional sense of that word. We’re trying to be recognizable to a specific group of people, the ones who feel like the platforms they helped build have moved on without them. 

If the film works, those people watch it once and know FrameRate is for them.

entry.title: Don't hold my hand: The new language of product launch films
entry.summary: "Wix Harmony - The New Way" exemplifies a shift in how digital products are debuted
entry.content:
While hanging out on FrameRate, I came across "Wix Harmony - The New Way", and it got me thinking about the current state of product launch films.

Old school: hold the viewer's hand through the interface

For a long time, the product launch video was essentially a guided tour. Cursor here, click there, watch this panel slide open, look at this dashboard. The job was to demonstrate. A brand system, if it existed at all, was decorative trim around a functional walkthrough.

That model assumed the audience didn't already know how software worked. It also assumed the most interesting thing about your product was your product.

New school: let the brand leak into the UI

What Wix Harmony does (and what a growing number of teams are doing) is invert that relationship. The brand design system isn't a frame around the product. It's the medium the product is shown through.

Watch what happens throughout the video.

  • A hover state fills with imagery from the brand system, not the real UI.

  • A prompt interface gets abstracted into a macro shot with chromatic aberration and vignetting.

  • When the user presses send, a ripple effect opens a portal that has nothing to do with how the actual button behaves.

You're oriented just long enough to know you're in Wix, then you're back to a curated lifestyle moment, a typographic flourish, a logo treatment.

The UI is the reference. The brand is the message.

Audiences are doing more of the work now

This only works because the audience has changed.

We've seen enough product launch videos to know the genre. We don't need a literal tour to understand we're being sold software, so the launch piece is free to be looser, more interpretive, more like a short film and less like a demo reel.

In "The New Way," the Angelica logo is the thread. It shows up on the opening frame and resurfaces enough times that you start clocking it without quite registering why.

That's a move you'd make in a music video, not a feature walkthrough. The team is trusting the viewer to bring attention, pattern recognition, and taste.

The product launch video used to ask: "What does this do?"

Now it asks: "Who is this for, and what world do they live in?"
