entry.title: A human-made response to the AI craze
entry.summary: Husband-and-wife team Julieta Tobon and Luis Mejia on rebirth and the title sequence they made for FITC Toronto
entry.content:
You can tell when a project has heart. There's an ineffable warmth that radiates from each frame.

But there's also an exquisite tension at work. On one side, there's imperfection and rawness, the mark of the human hand. And on the other side, there's an obvious obsession with getting every pixel and keyframe just right.

That's exactly what I felt when I sat in the audience at FITC Toronto and watched the opening titles from Escafandra Studio, the Toronto-based studio of Julieta Tobon and Luis Mejia.

The husband-and-wife team were kind enough to dive into the process behind their project, including their thinking on AI and the importance of hand-wrought craft.

How did this project come about?

Last year, we attended FITC. I had met Shawn [Pucknell, FITC founder and director] years prior, asking for some advice on running our local meetup (TOMO), so we decided to reconnect with him at the conference. We mentioned that we were interested in creating the titles for a future conference, and he asked us to email him.

Which we did! And around September, he reached out again, asking whether we were still interested and whether we wanted to pitch a concept for next year's conference. We certainly couldn't miss this opportunity, so we said yes! 

How did you develop the concept? Did you think in terms of a story? 

Yes! Before we came up with the story, we knew we wanted to do something different. In previous years, the FITC titles were these fully realized 3D masterpieces, which we loved! But we wanted to try something new. 

With the constant reminder of AI and the shiny new tools, we wanted to go “back to basics.” That was the first time we thought that this could work. After a couple of conversations with Shawn, we decided to “simplify” the concept in one word: Rebirth, a resurgence of analog tools and methods for design and animation.

Once we settled on that, we thought the best way to convey it was to follow the Principles of Design and Animation. We went forward with a story that started with a dot, which transformed into a line, then a plane (2D) and finally a volume (3D), but each segment would be informed by the previous one. In a sense, this represents the whole journey of our careers.

At what point did you start working with Jeff Moberg on the music and sound? 

We had collaborated with Jeff Moberg many times in the past and fully trust him, so we knew he was the right person for the job.

We reached out to him early on, when we had the concept and key art ready, along with a couple of music references. We were looking for a smooth progression from 50s jazz noir (in the 2D cel animation segment) to modern electronics (in the 3D segment). Once we had the Teaser fully animated (35 seconds), we sent it to him so he could do his magic!

His first draft blew us away; he undoubtedly elevated the piece to new heights!

Explain that process, please. How exactly did you collaborate? Did the music come first?

So, we usually start animation with a reference/placeholder stock track that has the vibe we’re looking for, and we had a conversation with Jeff about what we had in mind. That’s exactly what we did for the teaser. Then he composed the music and sfx and we used his new custom track for final delivery.

For the whole title sequence, we already had the foundation of the teaser, but now we had to transform 35 seconds of content into a full 2:30-minute sequence.

So, we focused on getting the design ready, and once we had enough content, Jeff provided us with a longer music track and a metronome to animate to.

We would send him every big animation update we had, so he could keep working on the music and sfx. It was an incredibly collaborative process; we worked closely with him, making sure every beat was in sync with every movement. He gave these titles so much life; we couldn’t have done it without him.

Once the animation was around 90% done, and we knew most of the timing was locked (we were only missing some polishing details), he went all in to finalize the music, including the final electronic crescendo that wasn’t part of the initial teaser.

Now let's talk about your approach to production. This has a very analog feel.

Was your production process 100% analog, or did you have some digital components to the workflow? 

Yes! We absolutely wanted the titles to feel analog. For us, it was essential to approach this project with a more tactile, artisanal approach.

There are, of course, digital components; we animated almost everything in After Effects, and the 3D sequences were done in Cinema 4D. We couldn't completely abandon the digital aspect. We wanted to achieve a marriage between analog and digital with seamless integration.

All the textures were made on paper with different markers, pencils and brushes. We also wrote the speakers' last names with markers, drawing them three times each, to create a loop animation instead of a static name. This process was a lot of fun!

The cel animations were done in Photoshop. And then the final edit and comp were done in After Effects.

But we didn't use any AI for this project. 😊

Was your decision to use such strong analog aesthetics a response to AI and the way it's changing the cultural conversation around creativity?

Definitely! Part of the write-up we did initially for FITC was: In a world moving too fast and overwhelmed by AI and shiny new tools, we want to pause, reflect, and bring back the concepts that inspired us as artists.

There’s this feeling that if you’re not working with AI or you don’t learn it right now, you’re going to be left behind. So, this is our response to that. You can still create fun and exciting things without AI, and hopefully, it resonates with people.

We didn’t coin this term, but someone called our titles “Human Made," and you know what, we feel really proud of that.

Do you have a favorite moment or sequence?  

Luis: It's too difficult to choose only one; this is our baby, so we love all of it. But for me personally, I took a good chunk of time creating a final 3D scene that could encompass everything we just watched, so I really like how we were able to create this 3D totem with 2D and cel animation elements on top.

Julieta: As Luis said, it's hard to choose just one, but I think the scene I had the most fun creating was the grid with the circles, because I just spent a lot of time matching every change of colour, texture and position with every beat of the music.

So satisfying to see, hahaha. Also, it was one of the first scenes we came up with, so it was with us throughout the whole process!

And of course, the zoetrope transitioning to the phenakistoscope is literally one of my favourite scenes as well! We wanted to bring these classic animation elements into the video, and it was so fun to figure out the timing and speed to make them move!

Tell us a little more about the full team that worked on this.

The initial concept, lookdev and key art were created by the two of us (Julieta and Luis). We wanted to make sure we had a solid foundation before bringing more people in, and from the moment we started planning these titles, we always knew we wanted a small team to help us get to the finish line.

Once it was time to work on the teaser, we reached out to Jeff Moberg to help us with the music and sound design.

After finishing the teaser and when it was time to work on the whole sequence, we reached out to a couple of close friends and artists here in Toronto to help us out.

Erin Prysiazny helped us design and animate a couple of sequences. She understood our vision and style and brought wonderful ideas to the table, especially the phenakistoscope.

John Flores, the “type” master, helped us animate all the names. We gave him the assets we had created for the last names, and he ran with them, adding the rest of the sans serif elements.

And James Johnson helped us test concepts for the 3D section near the end; we wanted to find a way to create 3D that felt connected to the 2D world and assets we had already established.

What's next for your studio? What kind of projects would you like to work on next? 

Oh, this is a great question! We are a fairly young studio, so we want to get the word out that we’re here, that we exist, and to continue collaborating with great people to create amazing work.

And, we are still riding the wave of this project, but we definitely want to work on more titles, not only for conferences but also for movies, TV shows, or games.

For now, we are collaborating with some local agencies in Toronto, and we hope to share more of the fulfilling work we are doing this summer.

As you said at your talk at FITC, we are riding our sailboat (pretty good thematically) and hoping to reach some exciting destinations next.

Thanks for taking the time to watch our titles and read a little bit more about our work.
